title: Seeing the same in all (13.19–13.34)
hook: one sun lights the whole world; chapter thirteen says one knower lights every field

segments.voice: Yesterday: knowledge and its opposite. A list of how to live, and the first item was humility. Your line was humility first. Did you let someone else be right? Today, the chapter's last and biggest picture. Day two hundred six.

Stand at a window at noon. The sun is lighting the street, the parked cars, the dog on the corner, the man you don't like who lives across the road, the trash can, the rose bush. All of it, at once, the same light. The sun doesn't choose. It doesn't get dirty from shining on the trash, and it doesn't get prettier from shining on the roses. Chapter thirteen ends with that exact picture. It's the Gita's answer to a question it has been circling all chapter: who is the knower of the field?
screen: `ONE SUN AT NOON.` → `THE ROSE AND THE TRASH CAN.` → `THE SAME LIGHT ON BOTH.`

segments.voice: First, two words the Gita uses a lot from here on. Prakriti: nature, everything that moves and changes, the body, the senses, the mind. Purusha: the person, the conscious one who experiences it. Verse twenty: nature is behind all doing, and the person is behind the experiencing of pleasure and pain. Then verse twenty-seven, the center of today. The one who sees the supreme Lord standing the same in all beings, not perishing when they perish, that one truly sees. Samam pashyan: seeing the same. Verse twenty-eight follows it: seeing the same Lord everywhere, such a person doesn't harm the self by the self. Think about that. If the same one lives in everyone, then hurting another is hurting yourself. Verse twenty-nine adds: the one who sees that nature does the acting, and that the self is not the doer, sees. Then two pictures to close the chapter. Verse thirty-two: space is everywhere, and because it's so subtle, it's never stained by what it holds. So the self in every body is never stained. And verse thirty-three: as the one sun lights up this whole world, so the knower of the field lights up the whole field. One light, many fields. The schools differ again on how literally to take the oneness: Advaita as one self, Vaishnava schools as one Lord dwelling in many selves. Either way, the practice is the same: look at anyone, and look for the light. That's the word today: seeing the same in all.
screen: `NATURE ACTS. THE PERSON KNOWS.` · `THE SAME LORD IN ALL BEINGS.` · `HARM NONE, HARM NOT YOURSELF.` · `ONE SUN LIGHTS THE WHOLE WORLD.` · then, large: `SEEING THE SAME IN ALL.`

segments.voice: Sit, and picture a light at your center, steady and warm. Now picture the person nearest you right now, in the next room or the next house. Picture the same light in them. Then someone across town. Then someone on the other side of the world whose name you'll never know. Then, if you're willing, someone you find hard. Same light. You don't have to like them. Just see the light. The bell holds the time.
Seeing the same in all. Gita thirteen, twenty-seven: the one who sees the same Lord standing in all beings, imperishable in the perishing, truly sees.
screen: `SEEING THE SAME IN ALL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the one light. Today, pick three strangers, a driver, a clerk, someone in line, and silently notice the same light in each. Day two hundred six.

howItsDone: Many Hindus greet others with namaste, often explained as honoring the divine in the other person; Gita 13.27–13.28, seeing the same Lord in all beings, is one of the verses teachers point to for this.

match.prompt: the chapter's last pictures — tap the pairs.

if the same one lives in all, harming another harms yourself.

verse 32: like space, it's so subtle it is never stained.

fork.setup: Krishna wants one picture for how the knower lights every field. what does he choose?
options: the one sun lighting the whole world.
a river flowing into the sea.
fork.reveal: the one sun. verse 33: as one sun lights this whole world, the knower of the field lights the whole field.

original.note: Sanskrit: sama, the same, even; in 13.28, 'samam pashyan', seeing the same everywhere.

trapdoor: what you thought: seeing the same in all means treating everyone identically.
what it means: seeing one light, the same Lord, in every being, so harming another harms yourself.
what a scholar hears: 13.27–13.28 use 'samam' twice; 13.32–13.33 give the images of space (akasha) and the one sun; Advaita and Vishishtadvaita read the oneness differently.
